what: An OLAP database like ClickHouse stores each column on its own, so it can sum, count and group billions of rows in well under a second. It powers dashboards and analytics, not single-row app reads.
like: Like a spreadsheet where you only pull out the one column you need to total, instead of photocopying every full row first.
why: Reads only the columns a query uses, so big scans stay fast
Columns of similar values compress far better than rows
Pre-aggregated rollups make dashboard queries tiny and instant

nodes.t: New data part|sorted by ORDER BY

steps.d: Your service buffers events, like one row per AI answer checked, and sends thousands at once. Each INSERT writes a new immutable data part on disk.
Inside the part, rows are sorted by the table's ORDER BY key and each column lives in its own compressed file, so a query touches only the columns it names.
The primary index keeps the key of just the first row of each granule (8,192 rows by default). It is tiny, fits in memory, and tells ClickHouse which granules to skip.
MergeTree keeps joining small parts into bigger sorted ones. That is why many tiny inserts hurt: merges cannot keep up and you get too many parts.
A materialized view runs on every inserted block and writes partial aggregates into a rollup table (SummingMergeTree or AggregatingMergeTree). Dashboards read thousands of rows instead of millions.
WHERE tenant_id = 42 AND day in last 30 matches the ORDER BY prefix, so only a few granules are read, decompressed and aggregated in parallel.

numbers.l: rows per granule by default; one index entry each
to scan 100 million rows in the docs' analytics example
rows per insert batch is ideal; at least 1,000
less disk than PostgreSQL for the same 100M-row benchmark
distinct values recommended for a partition key

choices.d: Put the columns you always filter on first, low cardinality before high: (tenant_id, day, engine). This decides which granules a query can skip, and cannot be changed cheaply later.
Usually by month, like toStartOfMonth(day). It is for data management - dropping old months, TTL, tiered storage - not for speed. Keep distinct values low.
Add a materialized view per hot dashboard shape (per tenant per day). Use -State functions in the view and -Merge functions when you query the rollup.
Batch 10,000-100,000 rows about once a second from a queue or buffer. If clients cannot batch, turn on async inserts so the server batches for you.
LZ4 by default for speed. ZSTD on cold or big text columns for smaller disk. Delta or DoubleDelta on timestamps.

instead.why: Transactions, updates and single-row reads; fine until analytics hits millions of rows
Managed warehouse for BI across many sources; less tuned for sub-second app dashboards
Metrics per series with retention; simpler when data is just numbers over time
Full-text search and relevance ranking rather than heavy aggregation

breaks.d: Thousands of tiny inserts each create a part and merges fall behind.
breaks.see: 'Too many parts' errors and a rising part count in system.parts
breaks.fix: Batch inserts, use async inserts, or put a queue like Kafka in front

breaks.d: Queries filter on a column the sort key does not start with, so nothing can be skipped.
breaks.see: EXPLAIN indexes=1 shows most granules selected; rows read close to table size
breaks.fix: Reorder the key to match filters, or add a projection or skip index

breaks.d: Partitioning by a high-cardinality column like user_id splits data into far too many parts.
breaks.see: 'Too many partitions for single INSERT block' and slow merges
breaks.fix: Partition by month or not at all; put user_id in ORDER BY instead

breaks.d: Averages of averages, or a view GROUP BY that does not match the target ORDER BY.
breaks.see: Dashboard totals differ from a query on the raw table
breaks.fix: Store -State aggregates, read with -Merge, and match GROUP BY to ORDER BY

breaks.d: Frequent single-row updates and deletes fight the append-and-merge design.
breaks.fix: Keep mutable data in Postgres; append new versions and use ReplacingMergeTree

say: Every check of whether an AI answer engine cites a brand is a fact row - that grows to billions fast, so I keep it in ClickHouse, not Postgres.
The table is a MergeTree ordered by (tenant_id, day, engine, prompt_id), so each customer's dashboard filter skips straight to its own granules.
A materialized view rolls facts into a per-tenant per-day table at insert time, so the dashboard reads thousands of rows, not millions.
Writers batch through a queue about once a second, and Postgres stays the source of truth for accounts and settings.

followups.q: Why not just add indexes in Postgres?
followups.a: Postgres reads whole rows and builds B-tree indexes for point lookups. A dashboard summing a few columns over millions of rows still drags every column off disk. ClickHouse reads only the needed columns, compressed around 10x smaller, and scans them in parallel.

followups.q: How do you keep tenants apart?
followups.a: Put tenant_id first in ORDER BY so every query filters on it and reads only that tenant's granules. Enforce it in the API layer, and add row policies or per-tenant users so one forgotten WHERE cannot leak data.

The smallest block ClickHouse reads: 8,192 rows by default. The sparse index stores the key of the first row of each granule, so it can binary-search to the few granules that might match and skip the rest.

followups.q: How do you handle late or corrected data?
followups.a: Append a new version row and use ReplacingMergeTree, which keeps the latest by a version column during merges. Read with FINAL or argMax when exact answers matter before merges finish.

check.q: A ClickHouse table gets 5,000 single-row inserts a second. What goes wrong first?
check.a: Too many parts, because merges cannot keep up
d: The sparse index runs out of memory
Queries start reading rows instead of columns
check.why: Each insert creates a part. Batch 10k-100k rows about once a second instead.

check.q: What does the sparse primary index store?
check.a: The key of the first row in each 8,192-row granule
d: A pointer to every single row
A hash of every column value
Only the minimum and maximum of the whole table
check.why: One entry per granule keeps the index tiny enough to live in memory.

check.q: Dashboards always filter by tenant and date. Best ORDER BY?
check.why: Leading with the filter columns lets the index skip other tenants' granules.

check.q: What is partitioning in ClickHouse mainly for?
check.a: Managing data, like dropping old months
check.why: The docs call it a data management tool. Speed comes from ORDER BY.
